newsitem.title: FRANCE: France's wounded Juppe says he is only human.
newsitem.headline: France's wounded Juppe says he is only human.

text.p: Prime Minister Alain Juppe, in an extraordinary plea for public sympathy, insisted on Tuesday he was more human than most French voters think and said there were no alternatives to his unpopular policies.
"I'd like people to realise that I'm not as technocratic as I may seem," Juppe said in a radio interview to present a book he wrote to complain that people are unfair to him.

In his 116-page "Entre Nous" (Between Ourselves), which went on sale on Tuesday, the 51-year-old Juppe sought to overturn his image as a brilliant but cold technocrat. He described himself as a scapegoat and admitted that the constant criticism hurts.

The least popular prime minister in modern French history, criticised for budget austerity that critics say has aggravated record 12.6 percent unemployment, Juppe said he believed better times were just around the corner.
"French (economic) growth in 1997 should be around 2.4 per cent," he told Europe 1 radio. "This is a floor not a ceiling."

He defended policies aimed at helping France qualify for a single European currency from 1999 and said his government's priority in the coming year would be to reduce unemployment, especially for the young.

He displayed the same unflinching resolution on Corsica. Welcoming the detention of hardline separatist leader Francois Santoni, who turned himself in to police on Monday, Juppe warned that the fight against violence on the French Mediterranean island would be long.
"Further attacks cannot be ruled out but they will not shake our determination," he said.
Ringingly confirmed in his post by President Jacques Chirac in a television interview last Thursday, Juppe said he expected to stay on until the 1998 general election, then leave office.
"My mission will be achieved by then," he said.
Often accused of being out of touch with everyday concerns, he said he was just like other human beings.

"Sometimes I eat, I sleep, I go for walks, I live," he said. "But when you are in government, you take the risk of saying things people don't want to hear. If I weren't able to defend my ideas, I'd do better to give up politics and go fishing."
Explaining why he wrote the book, Juppe said he was walking one day in Bordeaux, where he is the mayor, when a pretty woman walked towards him and shouted: "Death to the bloody idiot!'

"I was her target, there's no doubt. Pretty passer-by, I wanted to reply to you," Juppe wrote in his book, whose plain white cover patriotically uses red and blue lettering -- the colours of the French flag.
"Sometimes it gets tough but this (the book) is not about despair, it's about hope," he said.
Juppe said it was meeting Chirac, then prime minister, in 1976, which made him decide to go into politics.
"I was impressed by the man's strong presence," he recalled. "When I told him I was interested in politics, he asked me if I liked people. I felt he had asked the right question."
But people, as the book admits, are Juppe's problem. He acknowledges he is widely perceived as impatient, uncaring and superior but puts that down to his own shyness and stress.

He said he dashed off the book in his spare time on Sunday afternoons. But nothing was left to chance. A carefully orchestrated media plan to sell the new, human Juppe began with television and radio interviews.
And publishers NiL, who printed the two slim volumes that Chirac penned during his presidential campaign, are hoping Juppe's "love me" book will be a Christmas bestseller.
